title: PHAR 14 — Test
src: Drug Treatment of Asthma & Oral Side Effects

mcqs.q: Bronchial asthma is characterised by:
opts: Increased airway responsiveness with reversible narrowing
mcqs.explain: Asthma is increased responsiveness of the trachea/bronchi causing reversible airway narrowing, with inflammation underlying the hyperreactivity.

mcqs.q: The three abnormalities causing airflow impairment in asthma are:
opts: Bronchoconstriction, mucosal oedema and excess secretions
mcqs.explain: Airflow is impaired by bronchial smooth-muscle constriction, mucosal oedema and excessive bronchial secretions.

mcqs.q: Which analgesics should be AVOIDED in asthmatic patients?
mcqs.explain: NSAIDs and aspirin can trigger bronchospasm in asthmatics and should be avoided.

mcqs.q: The drug of choice to relieve an ACUTE asthma exacerbation is:
mcqs.explain: Inhaled salbutamol (β2-agonist) is the drug of choice for acute relief — bronchodilation within 5 minutes, lasting 2–4 hours.

mcqs.q: Inhaled salbutamol produces bronchodilation within about:
mcqs.explain: Inhaled salbutamol acts within ~5 minutes and its bronchodilator action lasts 2–4 hours.

mcqs.q: Theophylline causes bronchodilation by:
mcqs.explain: Theophylline (a methylxanthine) inhibits phosphodiesterase, raising cAMP and producing bronchodilation (plus cardiac stimulation).

mcqs.q: Theophylline toxicity (arrhythmia) can result when it is combined with:
opts: Ciprofloxacin or erythromycin (which raise its level)
mcqs.explain: Ciprofloxacin and erythromycin inhibit theophylline metabolism, raising its level toward toxicity; smoking, phenytoin and rifampicin lower it.

mcqs.q: Ipratropium bromide relieves asthma as a(n):
mcqs.explain: Ipratropium is an anticholinergic bronchodilator; salbutamol (β2) and theophylline (methylxanthine) are the other bronchodilators.

mcqs.q: Sodium cromoglycate is used ONLY for prophylaxis because it:
opts: Stabilizes mast cells but does not cause bronchodilation
mcqs.explain: Cromoglycate is a mast-cell stabilizer that inhibits mediator release; it does not dilate bronchi, so it is for prophylaxis, not acute attacks.

mcqs.q: Montelukast works by:
opts: Blocking airway leukotriene receptors (a preventer in persistent asthma)
mcqs.explain: Montelukast blocks leukotriene receptors, used as a preventer/adjunct in persistent asthma — not to terminate an attack.

mcqs.q: An example of an INHALED corticosteroid preventer is:
mcqs.explain: Beclomethasone is an inhaled corticosteroid; hydrocortisone is the systemic corticosteroid example.

mcqs.q: The MOST common oral side effect of medications is:
opts: Xerostomia (dry mouth) — over 250 drugs cause it
mcqs.explain: Xerostomia is claimed as a side effect by more than 250 medications (anticholinergics, antidepressants, antihistamines, diuretics, etc.).

mcqs.q: Reduced salivary flow predisposes to all of the following EXCEPT:
mcqs.explain: Decreased salivary flow INCREASES caries, fungal/bacterial infections, aphthous lesions and dysphagia — it does not reduce caries.

mcqs.q: Drug-induced xerostomia can be managed with:
mcqs.explain: Cholinergic agonists pilocarpine and bethanechol stimulate salivary flow and are used to manage drug-induced xerostomia.

mcqs.q: Drug-induced gingival enlargement is most commonly caused by:
mcqs.explain: Calcium-channel blockers (nifedipine), the anticonvulsant phenytoin and cyclosporine cause gingival overgrowth, related to dose and dental plaque.

mcqs.q: Treatment of drug-induced gingival enlargement includes:
opts: Stopping the offending drug, improving oral hygiene, and gingivectomy
mcqs.explain: Management is discontinuation of the drug, improved oral hygiene and, if needed, gingivectomy.

mcqs.q: Acute swelling (angioedema) of the lips/tongue is commonly caused by:
mcqs.explain: Penicillin, aspirin and NSAIDs are among the most common causes of acute, often transient, oral swelling (the lips most frequently).

mcqs.q: Oral mucositis and ulceration are particularly associated with:
mcqs.explain: Chemotherapeutic agents (methotrexate, 5-FU) commonly cause oral mucositis and ulceration.

mcqs.q: Burning mouth syndrome can be a side effect of:
mcqs.explain: ACE inhibitors and some antibiotics are associated with burning mouth syndrome.

mcqs.q: Red/orange discolouration of saliva and other body fluids may be caused by:
mcqs.explain: Levodopa and rifampicin can discolour saliva and other body fluids red/orange.

mcqs.q: Aphthous-like ulcers (systemic causes) may be produced by:
mcqs.explain: Aphthous-like ulcers can be caused by barbiturates, β-blockers and NSAIDs.

mcqs.q: Erythema multiforme (symmetrical mucocutaneous lesions) can be triggered by:
mcqs.explain: Erythema multiforme — symmetrical mucocutaneous lesions that may ulcerate — can be drug-induced by antibiotics and NSAIDs.

mcqs.q: Intrinsic asthma differs from extrinsic asthma in that it:
opts: Tends to be perennial, with status asthmaticus more common
mcqs.explain: Intrinsic asthma is perennial with status asthmaticus more common; extrinsic asthma is episodic and less prone to status asthmaticus.

mcqs.q: Why should a dentist take a thorough drug history?
opts: Many medications cause oral side effects affecting diagnosis and treatment
mcqs.explain: Because many prescription and OTC drugs affect the oral cavity (xerostomia, gingival enlargement, ulceration, candidiasis), a full drug history is essential.

saqs.q: List the three abnormalities causing airflow obstruction in asthma.
saqs.a: Bronchoconstriction (smooth muscle), mucosal oedema, and excessive bronchial secretions — from mast-cell mediators.

saqs.q: Name the asthma bronchodilator classes with an example of each.
Why is sodium cromoglycate used only for prophylaxis?
saqs.a: It is a mast-cell stabilizer that inhibits mediator release but produces no bronchodilation, so it cannot relieve an acute attack.

saqs.q: Give the key drug interaction of theophylline.
saqs.a: Ciprofloxacin and erythromycin inhibit its metabolism, raising the level → arrhythmia; smoking/phenytoin/rifampicin lower it.

saqs.q: Which drugs cause xerostomia and what are the consequences?
saqs.a: Anticholinergics, antidepressants, antihistamines, antipsychotics, diuretics (>250 drugs). Consequences: caries, fungal/bacterial infection, aphthous lesions, dysphagia.

saqs.q: Which drugs cause gingival enlargement and how is it managed?
saqs.a: Calcium-channel blockers (nifedipine), phenytoin, cyclosporine. Manage by stopping the drug, improving oral hygiene, gingivectomy.

saqs.q: Match oral effects to drug classes: gingival hyperplasia, xerostomia, candidiasis, mucositis.
